- When sentiment is strongly positive (≥ 0.17) in recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast by 1–3% for next period.  
- When sentiment is strongly negative (≤ -0.28), model often underestimates; increase forecast by 1–3% to compensate.  
- Model consistently overreacts to recent spikes (e.g., +5%+ in 3–5 days) — cap forecast rise to 2–4% after spike, then allow gradual mean reversion.  
- If true outcome shows mean reversion within 5–7 days after a peak, model often fails to correct — apply downward bias of 0.5–1.5% per day until reversion completes.  
- For 30-day horizon, model frequently overestimates early in the forecast window (first 5–7 days) — reduce first 3–5 forecast points by 1–2% to align with observed lag.  
- If sentiment history shows alternating +/– swings (e.g., +0.17, -0.28, +0.17), model tends to “smooth” extremes — adjust forecast to reflect sentiment volatility, not just average.  
- When true outcome is below 65–67, model often ignores downward pressure — apply a 0.5–1.5% downward bias if sentiment is neutral or negative.  
- If model forecast is > 75 and true outcome is < 72, reduce forecast by 2–4% for next 3–5 days unless sentiment is strong positive.  
- Model underestimates when sentiment is weak (0.00–0.06) — increase forecast by 0.5–1.5% if sentiment remains flat or slightly positive.
